cards.title: The online Boolean matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.context:
If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

cards.title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For example, imagine alternating long phases that repeatedly access two different small clusters of keys. A static layout must compromise between the clusters; an adaptive tree can reorganize between phases. The challenge is to pay for reorganization only when it is justified, even when an adversary changes the pattern. This is an illustrative example, not a new lower bound.

The 2026 analysis compares splaying directly to a moving optimal tree. Its remaining multiplicative factor still grows with n. Removing that factor would establish a universal constant-competitive guarantee, not merely another locality-sensitive upper bound.

cards.title: Can exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths be computed in truly subcubic time?
cards.formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least 2/3? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs O(1), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on O(log n)-bit index words cost O(1). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with one fixed positive exponent saving on all valid inputs, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists in the stated model. An n-cubed bound divided by a subpolynomial factor is progress but is not a positive answer.
cards.context:
Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.
cards.why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

cards.title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
cards.context:
Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.
cards.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
cards.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

cards.title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
cards.formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
cards.context:
An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.
cards.why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
cards.definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

cards.title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
cards.formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
cards.context:
A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
cards.definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.

progress.text: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant.
Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself.
The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.

cards.title: Can pointer-machine working-set heaps have constant amortized insertion and decrease-key?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most $C(M+\sum_{x\ \mathrm{extracted}}\log \Gamma(x))$? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define $\Gamma(x)=1+$ the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.
cards.definitions: Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one queue meeting the displayed total-cost bound for every sequence, or prove that every queue in this model has sequences with an unbounded ratio between its cost and that budget. Constant decrease-key with a growing insertion cost does not establish the positive answer. Neither does a word-RAM implementation using operations absent from the stated model.
cards.context:
The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.

Fast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum. Efficient extraction alone therefore does not settle the requested operation sequence bound.

The pointer restriction isolates the contribution of machine operations to this adaptivity. The July 2026 revision of van der Hoog and coauthors gives constant amortized insertion and working-set extraction, with inverse-Ackermann amortized decrease-key. That remaining factor is very slowly growing, but is asymptotically different from a constant.

A separate July 2026 construction achieves constant decrease-key with a stronger, stack-like extraction guarantee, while charging an iterated-log-star overhead to insertion. Its different trade-off is useful progress, but the joint constant-update target here still requires another argument. This card fixes the insertion-count definition of the working set and expresses the amortized question as a single total-cost inequality.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether temporal adaptivity and cheap priority changes can coexist without word-level machine tricks. A solution would clarify a model distinction in a fundamental graph-algorithm primitive. The small remaining factor makes it a sharper structural question than simply asking for a faster heap.

importance.reason: A concrete model-power gap for adaptive priority queues, with consequences for shortest-path methods that rely on both locality and cheap priority changes. It is more focused than general dynamic optimality.

cards.title: Does splaying every BST preorder take linear total time?
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that, for every n and every two binary search trees A and B on the same n distinct ordered keys, searching for the keys of preorder(B), in order, using bottom-up splaying starting from A costs at most Cn? Define preorder recursively as root, then left-subtree preorder, then right-subtree preorder. Every key is searched once. Charge one unit per visited search-path node and one per single rotation; perform no insertions or deletions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a universal linear bound for all pairs (A,B), or show that the ratio of this cost to n is unbounded over a family of such pairs. A bound requiring the traversal tree B to be balanced does not settle the proposition.
cards.definitions: A binary search tree stores one key per node, all left descendants smaller and all right descendants larger. On a search for x, first follow comparisons from the root to x. Then repeatedly splay x: if its parent is the root, rotate x over its parent (zig); if x and its parent are both left children or both right children, rotate the parent over the grandparent and then x over the parent (zig-zig); otherwise rotate x over its parent and then over its former grandparent (zig-zag). The same node x remains the splayed node until it becomes root. The arbitrary starting tree A and the tree B defining the permutation are separate inputs to the mathematical claim; splay receives only the search requests.
cards.context:
This asks about a particularly structured access sequence, rather than every possible sequence in the dynamic-optimality conjecture. A traversal visits each key exactly once, but its order reflects a second tree that may be quite different from the tree currently being searched. The proposed linear total bound says that this hidden structure is enough for splaying to adapt efficiently.

For example, the preorder of a balanced tree on seven keys can be 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7. This is not a sorted scan: after finishing one subtree, the sequence can jump to a distant part of the key order. If the starting tree is a long chain, even the first requested key can be far from the root. The question concerns the total cost, so a single expensive access is harmless if later savings pay for it.

The distinction between access and insertion matters. Building a tree by inserting the preorder keys into an empty splay tree is a different operation sequence, and that version is known to be linear. Linear access bounds are also known when the tree defining the preorder is weight-balanced. Neither restriction covers all traversal trees.

This is a useful intermediate target because the input family is precise and recognizable. A proof can exploit the recursive order of the permutation; a counterexample would have to show that this order still permits repeated expensive restructuring.
cards.why: I include this as a concrete test of whether a local restructuring rule detects global order in requests without being told that order. It isolates a major obstacle in understanding adaptive search trees while avoiding the full freedom of arbitrary repeated-access sequences.

progress.text: The traversal conjecture originates in the introduction of splay trees, as recorded in the later primary studies.
Levy and Tarjan prove linear-time preorder and postorder insertion into an empty tree, and linear access when the traversal tree is weight-balanced.

cards.title: Two anticomplete paths with unrestricted terminal pairing
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph G and four distinct pairwise nonadjacent vertices a,b,c,d, decides whether G contains two vertex-disjoint paths with no edge between their vertex sets, whose four endpoints are exactly a,b,c,d? Any of the three pairings of the four terminals is accepted.
cards.definitions: The input is an n×n adjacency matrix together with four vertex indices. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with an edge between each consecutive pair. The two paths must have disjoint vertex sets P and Q and satisfy E(G)∩(P×Q)=∅. Each terminal is the endpoint of exactly one path; none is an internal vertex. The accepted endpoint pairings are {ab,cd}, {ac,bd}, and {ad,bc}, with no prescribed source/sink partition. Paths can equivalently be required to be induced: replace either path by a shortest path between its endpoints in its own vertex set. This does not create an edge to the other path. Polynomial time means that one uniform deterministic Turing machine answers correctly on every valid input in at most C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k. Invalid encodings or nonindependent terminal sets are rejected by this formulation. There are no restrictions on the degree, genus, or connectivity of G.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such a polynomial-time algorithm with a proof, or prove that none exists. An NP-hardness proof for this exact unrestricted-pairing language would establish a negative answer under P≠NP, and must be labelled conditional accordingly. Hardness for a single prescribed pairing or for a prescribed source/sink partition is insufficient.
cards.context:
Ordinary disjoint routing prevents the paths from sharing vertices. Here even an unused graph edge between the two routes is forbidden. Thus one path must avoid the entire neighborhood of the other, and deciding which vertices to reserve can constrain a distant part of the graph.

The freedom to choose partners is the point of the question. Four terminals have three perfect pairings. A graph is accepted if at least one pairing works. A hard instance for a prescribed pairing may have an easy solution using another pairing; therefore simply invoking the hardness of any individual pairing does not classify their union.

The stable-terminal restriction isolates the unresolved case in Trotignon’s question. To see why an edge between two terminals helps, its endpoints would have to lie on the same solution path. That path can be shortened to the edge itself, leaving a reachability test for the remaining two terminals after deleting the closed neighborhoods of the first pair. Testing terminal edges handles these nonindependent cases.

This is a small routing primitive relevant to detecting induced minors, where a model must preserve both adjacency and nonadjacency between its connected pieces. An algorithm would allow a search to postpone the choice of which terminal belongs with which other terminal. A hardness proof would show that this flexibility still cannot overcome the anticompleteness constraint.

There are useful tractable restrictions. For graphs of any fixed bounded genus, polynomial algorithms for prescribed induced paths also solve this question by trying the three pairings. Conversely, the 2025 hardness theorem even for string graphs concerns prescribed pairs or a source/sink partition. The latter permits only two of our three pairings.
cards.why: This isolates a basic difference between specifying two routes and merely asking for two separated connections among four terminals. It is a compact test of how much freedom in terminal assignment can change the complexity of induced graph structure detection.

importance.reason: A concrete four-terminal primitive at the boundary of tractable routing and induced-containment hardness. Its importance comes from a missing basic complexity classification and its role in induced-minor detection, rather than from a large parameter range.

progress.text: The problem is in NP: the two vertex sequences form a certificate of length O(n log n), and adjacency, disjointness, terminal coverage, and absence of cross edges can all be checked in polynomial time. This is an immediate consequence of the stated definition, not a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

Trotignon explicitly asks for the complexity of the four-terminal problem with no prescribed pairing in Section 4.5 of the Dagstuhl report, printed page 140. The card makes its polynomial-time membership question explicit.

Aboulker, Bonnet, Picavet, and Trotignon prove NP-completeness for induced two-path routing even in a restricted class of string graphs. Their stronger flow theorem fixes two source terminals and two sink terminals. It does not automatically classify the language accepting all three perfect pairings.

The exact unrestricted-pairing question remains supported by its 2019 open-problem source. The checked recent theorem concerns different terminal constraints; no subsequent primary-source resolution of this exact question was located.

cards.title: Does recursively splitting a splay tree always take linear total time?
cards.formal: Start with an arbitrary n-node binary search tree. A split operation receives a current component tree and a key x in it, searches for x, splays x to that component’s root, and deletes x, leaving its left and right subtrees as separate components. Is the total cost of every legal sequence of n splits O(n)? Count all searches, rotations, and constant-time component bookkeeping. The input to each operation supplies the component’s root handle; identifying which component contains x is not a separate search problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal linear bound for every initial tree and legal split order, or prove that total cost divided by n is unbounded over such inputs. A bound with any unbounded multiplicative factor is partial progress.
cards.context:
Ordinary search adjusts one tree and keeps all its keys available. A split removes its accessed key and permanently separates the keys on its two sides. Subsequent operations happen independently in the resulting components. Every original key is accessed as a pivot exactly once, but it can participate in rotations caused by earlier pivots.

For example, splitting at the median key first separates the two halves of the key order. Continuing recursively with medians gives a balanced pattern of subproblems. Another legal sequence repeatedly chooses an extreme key and leaves almost the entire tree in one component. The conjecture must cover both, including mixtures chosen from different components.

There are only n requested pivots, which explains the linear target, but not a linear upper bound for the actual implementation. A key may lie deep in the current tree. The proof must show that restructuring work can be charged globally without repeatedly charging the same surviving material too much.

This differs from the deque conjecture: a deque deletes only an extreme, whereas a split may select any internal rank and produce two nonempty trees. The July 2026 analysis gives a new nearly linear bound for this splitting process, making the remaining multiplicative gap explicit.
cards.why: I include this because recursive partitioning is a basic way to organize ordered data. The conjecture asks whether splaying pays only for the number of objects eventually removed, regardless of the partition order. It is a sharply delimited test of the amortization techniques used for adaptive search trees.
cards.definitions: Keys have a fixed total order and are compared rather than arithmetically manipulated. Splaying uses zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations. Each key is removed exactly once; no insertions occur. The sequence can choose any currently nonempty component. The bound is a worst-case bound on total cost over complete sequences, not a per-split worst-case bound.

cards.title: Is 3-colorability polynomial-time decidable on diameter-two graphs?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map c:V(G)→{1,2,3} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv?
cards.definitions: The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under P≠NP. A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.
cards.context:
The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.

Bounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.

A tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

The best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to O(n^(1/3) log² n). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.
cards.why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.

Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.

cards.title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

cards.title: Can the final survivors of an offline heap sequence be found with linear comparisons?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic comparison algorithm and an absolute constant C that, for every legal sequence of N insert and delete-min operations starting from an empty priority queue, determines exactly which inserted items remain after the entire sequence using at most CN key comparisons? The complete operation sequence and all inserted keys are available before computation begins. Only the final membership vector is required; the algorithm need not output the items removed at intermediate delete-min operations or their removal order.
cards.definitions: Each insert introduces a distinct item with a key in an opaque totally ordered universe; all inserted keys are pairwise distinct. A delete-min removes the currently present item of smallest key. Legality means that in every prefix the number of delete-min operations is at most the number of inserts. If I is the total number of inserts, the output is an I-bit vector in insertion order, marking exactly the items still present after all N operations. The algorithm may examine any part of the input sequence at any time. Its only access to key values is by pairwise order comparisons; operation positions and item identities carry no information about key order. Count every key comparison, including preprocessing comparisons. Ordinary computation on indices and comparison outcomes is not the cost measure, but the algorithm must terminate and be correct on every input.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform deterministic algorithm meeting the CN comparison bound for every legal sequence, or prove that every such algorithm requires a superlinear number of comparisons on a family of inputs. Sorting all removed items or simulating the queue online would solve stronger tasks; a lower bound for those stronger tasks is not a negative answer here.
cards.context:
A usual priority queue must identify each minimum when the corresponding request arrives. The offline task can postpone every decision and return only a final set. For example, after insert(8), insert(2), delete-min, insert(1), the survivors are 8 and 1. This is not simply the set of the two largest inserted keys: 2 disappeared before 1 became available. The interleaving still matters even though the intermediate outputs are discarded.

One upper bound is to simulate a comparison heap and mark its remaining elements, using O(N log(N+2)) comparisons. At the other extreme, when all insertions precede all deletions, one linear-time selection suffices to find the surviving upper part of the key order. The question asks whether arbitrary temporal interleaving can be handled without losing that linear comparison bound.

The ordinary heap sorting lower bound depends on recovering the entire order of the extracted keys. Here, if I items were inserted, there are at most 2^I possible membership vectors. Counting outputs therefore does not give the usual factorial number of leaves needed for sorting. This observation only removes one lower-bound argument: a small output space by itself is not a construction of a shallow comparison decision tree.

A successful approach can exploit future deletions and later insertions, because the complete schedule is known. It need not maintain any particular heap representation. That freedom makes the problem a useful test of how much information an algorithm really needs when only a summary of a dynamic process is requested. The formulation deliberately asks about comparisons, leaving a linear total running time as a stronger goal.
cards.why: This isolates a basic gap between maintaining a dynamic process and computing its final outcome. It connects offline data structures with selection and comparison lower bounds, in a small enough model that both algorithms and adversaries can be stated precisely.

importance.reason: A clean offline-versus-online information question for the priority-queue primitive. It could reveal a general way to avoid reconstructing unneeded intermediate outputs, while remaining narrower than model-wide dynamic lower bounds.

cards.title: Can an acyclic subgraph preserve a constant fraction of the optimal reachable pairs?
cards.formal: For a finite directed graph G=(V,E), let $R(D)=|\{(u,v)\in V^2:u\ne v,\text{ a directed path from }u\text{ to }v\text{ exists in }D\}|$ and $\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\max\{R((V,F)):F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ is acyclic}\}$. Do there exist a constant alpha>0 and a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in |V|+|E| that, for every G, outputs F subset E with (V,F) acyclic and R((V,F)) >= alpha OPT(G)? The constant and polynomial exponent must be independent of G. This card selects constant-factor approximation as a precise target within the source’s broader optimization question.
cards.definitions: The input is an adjacency-list representation of an unweighted directed graph with labeled vertices 1,...,n, no self-loops, and at most one edge for each ordered pair. Oppositely directed edges may both be present. The algorithm may delete edges but may not add edges, reverse edges, identify vertices, or remove vertices. Reachability uses paths of positive length and counts ordered pairs of distinct vertices, not paths or retained edges. An acyclic graph has no directed cycle. Output is the list of retained edges. Polynomial time is measured in ordinary bit operations on the finite input; no oracle for reachability or optimization is free. When OPT(G)=0, any acyclic output satisfies the value requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time algorithm and prove one universal positive approximation ratio, or prove that no algorithm with the quantified guarantee exists. A conditional impossibility result must identify its complexity assumption. Guarantees on the number or weight of deleted edges, or empirical similarity to a reference hierarchy, do not establish the required guarantee on reachable pairs.
cards.context:
A directed edge can represent a declared relation between two concepts, while a path represents an implied relation. Removing one edge can therefore erase many implications even if almost every input edge remains. The objective counts the implications preserved after all cycles have been removed. The optimum in the denominator already obeys acyclicity, so the algorithm is not asked to retain mutually contradictory reachability in both directions.

For example, a directed path on n vertices has only n-1 edges but n(n-1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. Deleting a middle edge destroys roughly a quarter of all n^2 ordered pairs. Conversely, adding a shortcut between vertices that are already connected by a path increases the edge count without adding a new reachable pair. These examples explain why edge-count approximation guarantees cannot simply be reused for this objective.

Ajwani’s 2016 question asks for an acyclic edge subgraph whose transitive closure has maximum size, motivated by cleaning taxonomies assembled from multiple contributors. The source explicitly welcomes approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics but specifies no approximation threshold. The constant alpha target here is an editorial specialization, rather than an approximation conjecture quoted from the seminar.

The 2017 follow-up on noisy hierarchies develops practical cycle-removal heuristics and evaluates recovery of inserted noisy edges. It identifies deviation in transitive closure as a possible further measure. Those experiments do not provide a worst-case ratio for R(D). A 2026 ranking paper likewise uses reachability to make edge reinsertion cycle-safe, but optimizes edge-weight disagreement; that use of reachability does not turn its objective into this one.

cards.title: Does ordinary median-of-medians selection with groups of three run in linear time?
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that the fixed deterministic comparison algorithm Select3 below uses at most Cn key comparisons on every sequence A of n distinct ordered keys and every requested rank $1\le k\le n$? Its output must be the k-th smallest key. The question concerns the one-grouping-pass algorithm exactly as specified; all recursive pivot-selection comparisons count toward the same cost.
cards.definitions: Define Select3(A,k) as follows. If |A| <= 3, sort a copy by insertion sort and return its k-th element. Otherwise put the first $3q$ elements, where $q=\lfloor |A|/3\rfloor$, into consecutive disjoint triples. Obtain each triple's median by sorting a copy using compare-exchanges (1,2), (2,3), (1,2); this leaves A unchanged. Let B be these q medians in group order. Set $p=\mathrm{Select3}(B,\lceil q/2\rceil)$. Scan all of A, including its at most two ungrouped final elements, comparing each key with p and forming L of keys below p and R of keys above p, preserving their original order. If k=|L|+1 return p; if k<=|L| return Select3(L,k); otherwise return Select3(R,k-|L|-1). One comparison returns the relative order of two keys at unit cost. The algorithm stores subsequences explicitly and uses no randomization, arithmetic on keys, or reuse of comparison outcomes beyond this description. These rounding and base-case conventions make the source's algorithm fully specified.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated comparison bound for every input sequence and every requested rank, or give a family of inputs and ranks for which comparisons divided by n are unbounded. An O(n log n) upper bound alone is not a refutation of linear time. A different small-group selection algorithm is not a positive answer for Select3.
cards.context:
Selection asks for one position in sorted order without requiring the whole sorted sequence. The pivot controls how much work can be discarded: after finding it, only the side containing the requested rank is relevant. Here the pivot itself must be selected recursively from the medians of small groups. Its quality and the cost of obtaining it therefore have to be analyzed together.

The familiar three-group analysis bounds two recursive subproblems by roughly n/3 and 2n/3, plus a linear scan. This gives an O(n log n) upper bound. It does not exhibit an input on which both recursive calls repeatedly realize their separate worst cases. They are linked: the median list is made of elements from the very array that is partitioned. An adversarial construction cannot freely choose the two subproblems independently.

A useful distinction is between the grouping size and the number of grouping passes. The repeated-step method groups the medians into triples again before selecting a pivot recursively. That modified algorithm has a linear-time analysis, but it makes a different recursive call from Select3. The present question preserves the simpler, single-pass rule.

For a proof attempt, the stable ordering in L and R matters because it determines the triples at the next call. Fixing these details turns an informal discussion of small groups into one mathematical proposition. A positive answer would establish that the standard recurrence loses an asymptotic factor; a negative answer must capture actual coupled executions, rather than just solve the upper-bound recurrence.
cards.why: This is a compact fundamental algorithm-analysis problem: even for a textbook primitive, independently worst-case recursive bounds may not be simultaneously attainable. It provides a concrete place to develop sharper tools for dependent subproblems or an explicit adversary.

cards.title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
cards.formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
cards.definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
cards.context:
A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.
cards.why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.

cards.title: Does the expected redundancy of optimal alphabetic trees with random weights converge?
cards.formal: For each n >= 2, let $D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)$ be uniform on the probability simplex, equivalently Dirichlet(1,...,1). Let $C_n(D)=\min_T\sum_{i=1}^n D_i d_T(i)$, where T ranges over full ordered binary trees with leaves 1,...,n in that left-to-right order and d_T(i) is the depth of leaf i, with root depth zero. Define $H(D)=-\sum_iD_i\log_2D_i$ and $r_n=\mathbb E_D[C_n(D)-H(D)]$. Does the real sequence r_n converge to a finite limit as n tends to infinity? This is a precise limit-existence target within the source’s broader request to determine the expected optimal cost.
cards.definitions: A full binary tree has exactly two children at every internal node. An ordered tree distinguishes left from right, and the fixed leaf order is the alphabetic constraint. Following left and right edges as bits gives an alphabetic prefix code: no leaf codeword is a prefix of another, and lexicographic codeword order agrees with symbol order. The tree is optimized separately after the probabilities D are realized; the expectation is taken afterward. To sample D, draw n-1 independent uniform points in (0,1), sort them, append endpoints 0 and 1, and take the n successive interval lengths. The weights are positive almost surely. For a fixed D, the cost is the expected number of binary decisions to find a leaf drawn with probabilities D; no random-tree distribution is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every epsilon > 0 there exists N0 such that |r_n-r_m| < epsilon for all n,m >= N0, or prove that this Cauchy property fails. A negative answer can be established by separated subsequential limits. Identifying the numerical value of a limit, if it exists, is useful further progress but is not required for the stated yes/no question. Bounded redundancy or finite Monte Carlo estimates alone do not settle convergence.
cards.context:
An alphabetic tree preserves the order of the symbols, so a search can branch according to comparisons with boundaries in that order. This constraint is useful for searching and ordered merging, but can prevent the tree from using exactly the codeword lengths it would choose if the symbols were freely permutable. Redundancy measures the extra expected decisions beyond the entropy lower bound.

There are two levels of averaging. Once the weights are fixed, the weighted leaf depths describe the cost of queries to one optimized tree. The question then averages that optimum over a random probability vector. Optimizing a tree for the mean weight vector would be a different operation: it would choose a tree before seeing which symbols are common in the realized distribution.

The standard alphabetic coding bound gives 0 <= C_n(D)-H(D) < 2, so r_n is bounded. Boundedness does not imply convergence. Integer codeword lengths make it especially important not to assume that a constant correction term exists without proof. The present target isolates that issue before asking for the complete expected-cost formula.

Its broad formulation asks to compute or approximate the expectation. This card extracts the specific convergence question explicitly; it does not attribute a conjectured limit or a claimed asymptotic formula to the source.

cards.title: Can four-sided skyline reporting match ordinary range reporting?
cards.formal: Preprocess a static set $P\subseteq[N]^2$ of $N$ points, with distinct coordinates in each dimension, on a word RAM with $\Theta(\log N)$-bit words. Is there a structure using $N\log^{O(1)}N$ words that reports the skyline of $P\cap([a,b]\times[c,d])$ in worst-case $O(\log\log N+k)$ time, where $k$ is the number of reported points? A point is on the skyline if no other point in the query rectangle is at least as large in both coordinates and strictly larger in one.
cards.context:
Think of records scored on two attributes, with larger values preferred. A range filter first selects the eligible records; the skyline then removes options that are worse on both attributes. For points (1,5), (3,3), (4,4), and (5,1), the full-set skyline excludes (3,3). A rectangle that includes (3,3) but cuts off (4,4) can make it a skyline point. Therefore, storing only the global skyline loses information needed for later queries.

The output can be much smaller than the number of points inside the rectangle. If a rectangle contains thousands of points and one dominates all others, the requested bound permits only $O(\log\log N)$ time beyond outputting that one point. Reporting every point and filtering afterward cannot meet it. The data structure must skip large dominated regions without paying for their contents.

Counting and reporting have different targets. Four-sided skyline counting needs $\Omega(\log N/\log\log N)$ query time at near-linear space. That does not directly refute fast reporting: counting by enumeration costs an additional $k$, which can be large. The known reporting upper bound pays the same logarithmic overhead as counting, plus the output size.

The 2026 paper distinguishes the top-open and bottom-open three-sided variants and explicitly leaves the four-sided reporting bound unresolved. The missing side of a rectangle can change the problem, so results for three-sided queries do not settle this card.
cards.why: This asks whether selecting only undominated answers imposes an inherent indexing cost beyond locating a range and emitting its output. I include it as a focused data-structure problem with a precise model, a concrete gap, and a useful distinction between counting, reporting, and output-sensitive computation.

Coordinates are already in rank space; this avoids hiding a separate predecessor-search cost for a larger universe. The set is static. Space is measured in machine words, not bits. The factor $\log^{O(1)}N$ has a fixed exponent. The output parameter $k$ is query-dependent, and no scan of all of $P\cap Q$ is allowed unless its cost fits the stated bound.

The target is deterministic exact reporting with polynomial preprocessing time, using the usual word-RAM operations: arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words.

cards.title: Can lazy B-tree priority queues keep their I/O bounds with stable handles?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic comparison-based external-memory priority queue with a universal constant c of internal storage at most cB words that satisfies the following bounds for every capacity $N\ge B\ge2$? Starting empty and never holding more than N elements, it uses $O(1+N/B)$ external blocks, supports insertion and handle-based decrease-key in $O(1+\log_B\log_B N)$ worst-case I/Os, and supports extract-min in $O(1+B^{-1}\log_2 N+\log_B\log_B N)$ amortized I/Os. Every handle remains valid until its element is removed. All handle maintenance and lookup costs count. Each logarithm is truncated below at one.
cards.context:
A handle lets an algorithm change a particular queued object after that object has moved. For example, a graph algorithm may keep a reference to a vertex’s queue entry and lower its priority when a better route is discovered. The reference must still identify that entry after other insertions, extractions, and internal rearrangements.

Block transfers make this subtle. Moving $B$ consecutive records between a few blocks can cost only a constant number of I/Os. If each record has a reference stored in a different disk block, repairing those references can cost $\Theta(B)$ I/Os. An analysis of the records alone can therefore miss the operation that dominates the running time.

Adding an indirection table is a possible design choice, not a complete solution. It can keep the caller’s handle stable, but the structure must update the table when entries move and look up the correct location on later decreases. Those accesses can again be scattered. The question requires charging these costs to the same operation bounds.

The December 2025 revision explicitly corrects the conference claim about priority-queue performance. It identifies the cost of external references as unaccounted for and reports logarithmic extract-min cost for the straightforward implementation when every element has a reference.
cards.why: I include this because stable object identity is part of a data structure’s interface, and its cost can conflict with the locality that makes external-memory algorithms fast. The target is specific enough to attack with a representation or a lower bound, while the obstruction also matters for other structures that move records in blocks.
cards.definitions: One I/O transfers B consecutive words between internal and external memory. N is an announced upper bound on the number of live elements, fixed for the operation sequence. Words contain O(log N) bits; keys and handles occupy a constant number of words, and key values are accessed by comparisons. A returned handle must continue identifying the same object after internal relocation. Decrease-key receives a handle and a no-larger priority; extract-min returns and removes an element with minimum priority. All auxiliary tables count toward the space bound. Amortized extract-min cost means that total cost of any legal sequence is bounded by the sum of its stated operation budgets.

progress.text: Eenberg, Larsen, and Yu establish a general external-memory lower bound showing that adding decrease-key can increase priority-queue cost. This is background on the resource tradeoff; it does not resolve the particular handle-sensitive bounds on this card.

The revised Lazy B-Trees paper records the missing pointer cost. Its displayed priority-queue bounds explicitly exclude that cost, and therefore are not a solution to the fully charged interface above.

cards.title: Succinct dynamic rank/select in a polynomial universe — resolved
cards.formal: Can a dynamic set S⊆{0,…,U−1}, with n=|S| and polynomially larger universe U=n^(1+Θ(1)), be represented using H(n,U)+o(H(n,U)) bits while supporting insertion, deletion, rank and select in deterministic O(1+log n/log log(n+2)) worst-case time per operation on a word RAM with multiplication and word size Θ(log U)? Here H(n,U)=log₂ binom(U,n). Yes: Domingues’s 2026 construction implies this bound.
cards.definitions: Fix any constants δ>0 and K≥1+δ. The bounds must hold uniformly whenever n≥2 and n^(1+δ)≤U≤n^K, with constants allowed to depend on δ,K. U is fixed during an operation sequence and n may change by one per update; both endpoints of each update are in the stated regime. Insert(x) adds an absent key, Delete(x) removes a present key, Rank(x)=|{y∈S:y≤x}| for any x∈{0,…,U−1}, and Select(j) returns the j-th smallest key for 1≤j≤n. Invalid select arguments return a failure symbol. These are set updates, not insertions that shift the positions of a bit string. The machine has w=⌈log₂(U+1)⌉-bit words and unit-cost reads/writes, comparisons, addition/subtraction, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts and word multiplication. All operations are exact, deterministic and terminating. Initialization from the initial set may take polynomial time in U. Space uses the M_B convention: unused gaps below the highest allocated address count, including partially used final words. Count all stored metadata and lookup tables; a fixed table of polylog(w) words computable from w is allowed and fits in the asymptotic redundancy here. No free input-dependent advice is provided. During an update use the larger of the pre- and post-update space budgets. Succinctness means that the redundancy divided by H(n,U) tends to zero uniformly over the fixed polynomial regime.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical existence target is resolved affirmatively with deterministic worst-case operations. This does not assert o(n) redundancy at that same deterministic worst-case time, nor a bound for every universe density. The precise target is vanishing redundancy relative to H(n,U).
cards.context:
Rank translates a key into its position in sorted order, while select translates a position back into a key. Together they support predecessor search and form an interface used inside compressed representations. A fully indexable dictionary must answer rank even when the queried key is absent, which is stronger than an index that only accepts stored keys.

There are binom(U,n) possible sets of a fixed cardinality, so H(n,U) bits is the basic information requirement. A conventional search tree also stores navigation information and counts, whose overhead can be substantial. Succinctness asks for a representation whose extra bits become a negligible fraction of that information requirement.

The word “succinct” needs its formula. In the polynomial-universe regime here, H is Θ(n log n). An overhead of n times a fractional power of log n is therefore succinct even though it exceeds n bits. The 2025 source uses relative redundancy as its definition; silently replacing that target by o(n) extra bits would create a stronger question.

Static indexing can inspect the entire set once and organize an elaborate compressed representation. Updates must preserve both the indexing information and the encoding as the set changes. The 2025 static FID result explicitly left the dynamic time-and-space combination as a separate question.

Two subsequent results address different guarantees. The SODA 2026 construction gets much smaller redundancy with amortized expected operation time. Domingues’s construction gives deterministic worst-case time with a larger but still negligible relative overhead. The latter directly answers the stronger time convention fixed in this card.
cards.why: Rank/select is a basic ordered-data interface. Achieving its optimal dynamic time together with near-minimum encoding space shows that compression need not cost an additional asymptotic slowdown, and distinguishes space spent on information from space spent on navigation.

importance.reason: A basic time-space frontier for a widely used ordered-data primitive. The historical existence question is now resolved; its importance is preserved while resolved cards sort below open candidates.

progress.text: Liang and Zhou give optimal static FID trade-offs and explicitly leave succinct dynamic FIDs with O(log n/log log n) operation time open for polynomial universes. Their definition of succinctness is redundancy o(H), not necessarily o(n).

Kuszmaul, Liang, and Zhou give dynamic insert/delete/rank/select with optimal amortized expected time and redundancy n/2^((log n)^Ω(1))+polylog U in the polynomial regime. This addresses the earlier existence question with randomized amortized guarantees.

Domingues’s Theorem 1 gives deterministic worst-case O(1/ε+log_w n) operations with H+O(n w^ε/ε) bits and a polylog(w)-word table. The construction also supports selecting zero bits in the complement.

Set ε=1/4 and w=Θ(log U)=Θ(log n). The redundancy is O(n(log n)^(1/4))+polylog(log n), which is o(n log n)=o(H), and log_w n=Θ(log n/log log n). Thus the theorem supplies exactly the required deterministic worst-case succinct structure.

cards.title: Multipass pairing heaps: logarithmic amortized delete-min — resolved
cards.formal: Does the standard multipass pairing heap satisfy the following bound? For every valid operation sequence starting with no heaps, let D be the number of delete-min operations, Q the number of all other operations, and N the maximum size of any heap during the sequence. The total number of key comparisons and constant-time pointer operations is at most C[Q + D log₂(N+2)] for a universal C. Allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld and delete-min. The answer is yes, as a consequence of Sinnamon and Tarjan’s theorem.
cards.definitions: Keys are opaque elements of a total order, with distinct keys for simplicity. A nonempty heap is one rooted ordered tree with each parent key smaller than its children’s keys; its root is the minimum. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger-key root the leftmost child of the smaller-key root. Insertion links a singleton with the existing root, or creates the root if empty. Melding consumes two disjoint heaps and links their roots, with empty heaps handled directly. find-min returns the root key. delete-min removes the root and treats its children, in their current left-to-right order, as roots. A pass links the first and second roots, the third and fourth, and so on; an unpaired final root carries over unchanged. The surviving roots remain in their relative order. Repeat complete passes from left to right until at most one root remains. Sibling lists and child pointers support each link in O(1) pointer operations. Valid delete-min and find-min calls use nonempty heaps. N=0 is allowed for sequences containing no inserted item. The bound is over the whole sequence, including a sequence ending with nonempty heaps. Decrease-key is excluded from this precise basic bound; its separate cost is discussed below.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical target is the stated universal sequence bound for this exact pairing schedule. It has been proved. A single delete-min need not take O(log N) actual time; the logarithmic guarantee is amortized across the operation sequence.
cards.context:
Self-adjusting heaps rearrange their trees in response to operations without storing balance ranks or subtree sizes. The multipass rule is especially simple: remove the minimum, pair adjacent roots repeatedly, and retain the smaller root in each pair. The absence of explicit balancing makes the implementation short, but conceals how much future work a link creates.

An individual minimum can have many children. Removing that root therefore may require a linear number of links, even though each pairing pass approximately halves the root list. Counting the number of passes alone does not prove a logarithmic operation cost. The analysis must account for links over an entire sequence.

The 2018 paper reduced the extra factor above logarithmic amortized cost to a very slowly growing expression involving the iterated logarithm. That was a meaningful improvement in the analysis, but it still did not give the exact logarithmic target. The same paper also studies path-balanced search trees; those are a separate algorithm and question.

Sinnamon and Tarjan subsequently obtained logarithmic amortized delete-min, constant-time insertion and melding, and stronger bounds that discount items never deleted. Their theorem also allows decrease-key operations, charging them separately. The displayed formulation keeps only the basic operations so that the claim about delete-min cannot accidentally promise free decrease-key.

This remains in the catalogue as a resolved historical card. It documents how a long-standing analysis problem was settled without changing the familiar multipass algorithm. Keeping the exact pairing order also prevents confusion with the standard two-pass pairing heap, whose second pass accumulates links differently.

The multipass rule is especially simple: remove the minimum, pair adjacent roots repeatedly, and retain the smaller root in each pair. The absence of explicit balancing makes the implementation short, but conceals how much future work a link creates.

An individual minimum can have many children. Removing that root therefore may require a linear number of links, even though each pairing pass approximately halves the root list. Counting the number of passes alone does not prove a logarithmic operation cost. The analysis must account for links over an entire sequence.

The 2018 paper reduced the extra factor above logarithmic amortized cost to a very slowly growing expression involving the iterated logarithm. That was a meaningful improvement in the analysis, but it still did not give the exact logarithmic target. The same paper also studies path-balanced search trees; those are a separate algorithm and question.

Sinnamon and Tarjan subsequently obtained logarithmic amortized delete-min, constant-time insertion and melding, and stronger bounds that discount items never deleted. Their theorem also allows decrease-key operations, charging them separately. The displayed formulation keeps only the basic operations so that the claim about delete-min cannot accidentally promise free decrease-key.

This remains in the catalogue as a resolved historical card. It documents how a long-standing analysis problem was settled without changing the familiar multipass algorithm. Keeping the exact pairing order also prevents confusion with the standard two-pass pairing heap, whose second pass accumulates links differently.
